idea.body: Counting arrangements cares about order, counting selections does not. Choosing a first and second place winner from racers A, B and C gives 6 orders: AB, BA, AC, CA, BC, CB. That is a permutation. Choosing 2 of those same racers for the next round, with no ranking, gives only 3 pairs. AB and BA are now the same pair. That is a combination. A combination count is always a permutation count divided by the ways to order the chosen items among themselves. Every over-count gets removed exactly once.

figure.alt: A table of outcomes choosing 2 of the letters A, B, C. Six arrangements, since order matters, but only three selections, since order does not.

workedExample.prompt: A game has 8 available characters. In how many ways can a player choose a main and a backup character, in order? Separately, in how many ways can a player just choose 2 characters, with no roles?
steps: Choosing a main and a backup is a permutation, since the two roles are different.
There are 8 choices for the main character and 7 left for the backup: 8 times 7 is 56.
Choosing 2 characters with no roles is a combination instead.
Each pair was counted twice in the permutation count, once for each order, so divide 56 by 2.
56 divided by 2 is 28.

ways.name: The slots
ways.when: Use this default method for any question where the order of the choices matters.
steps: Draw one slot for each role: main, then backup.
Fill the main slot: 8 choices are available.
Fill the backup slot: one character is already used, so 7 choices remain.
Multiply the slots together: 8 times 7 is 56.
ways.example: 8 characters are available. Choose a main and a backup character, in order.
ways.trap: Using 8 choices for both slots instead of one fewer for each after the first.

ways.name: The tree
ways.when: Use this to see every order laid out as a branching path.
steps: Draw a tree: the first branch picks first place, from A, B or C.
From each first choice, branch again for second place, using the two remaining racers.
Follow every path from the start to an end: each path is one order.
Count the ends: 3 times 2 is 6, so 6 orders.
ways.example: Choose a first and second place winner from racers A, B and C.
ways.trap: Forgetting to remove the already-used racer from the second set of branches.

figure.alt: A tree of first and second place orders for racers A, B and C, branching to 6 outcomes.

ways.name: Divide out the order
ways.when: Use this when the choices have no separate roles, so each group is counted twice or more.
steps: First count the ordered choices, as if the two picks had roles: 8 times 7 is 56.
Each unordered pair was counted twice in that total, once for each order.
Divide the ordered count by the number of ways to order 2 items, which is 2.
56 divided by 2 is 28.
ways.example: 8 characters are available. Choose 2 characters, with no roles.
ways.trap: Forgetting to divide and leaving the answer as the larger ordered count, 56.

ways.name: The formula
ways.when: Use this when you want a direct formula instead of building slots every time.
steps: Use the combination formula: n choose r is n! divided by r! times (n - r)!.
Here n = 6 and r = 3, so it is 6! divided by 3! times 3!.
6! is 720, and 3! is 6, so the denominator is 6 times 6, which is 36.
720 divided by 36 is 20.
ways.example: Choose 3 of 6 pizza toppings, with no order.
ways.trap: Mixing up the permutation and combination formulas and forgetting to divide by r!.
